to see
This verb, like βλέπω [to see], corresponds to Latin video or cerno and is used of what is perceived either by the eyes or by the mind, noticed, understood.
ὁράω [to see] — I see.

The remaining tenses of this verb are taken partly from itself and partly from other verbs, whose present tenses are not in use but have been invented by grammarians. Of the present ὁρῶ [I see], besides the indicative, Aeschylus used the imperative ὅρα [see!], the infinitive ὁρᾶν [to see], and the participle ὁρῶν [seeing]. No examples of the imperfect ἑώρων [I was seeing] or the perfect ἑόρακα [I have seen] are found in him. When the perfect was needed, the tragedians used the more poetic and metrically suitable form ὄπωπα [I have seen], of which seven examples are found in Sophocles, and one in Aeschylus, Eum. 57. The aorist εἶδον [I saw] is very common, with its other moods ἴδε [see!], ἴδοιμι [may I see], ἴδω [I may see], ἰδεῖν [to see], ἰδών [having seen]. The second person singular of the imperative, written ἴδε [see!], is read three times in Sophocles, OC. 1462 and with elision Tr. 222, 821; in Aeschylus it is read once, Suppl. 349, and with elision it has been restored by me at Pr. 542 ἴδ᾽ ὅπως [see how] for φέρ᾽ ὅπως [bring how], about which I spoke in the Preface to the London edition of 1866, p. XIV. Herodianus vol. 1 p. 431, 5, vol. 2 p. 23, 22 ed. Lentz teaches that among the Attics, like λαβέ [take!], it is oxytone idé. The future is ὄψομαι [I will see]. || Passive ὁρῶμαι [I am seen] with perfect ὦμμαι [I have been seen], whose third person ὦπται [he has been seen] is read at Pr. 998 (there are no examples of the aorist ὤφθην [I was seen] or the future ὀφθήσομαι [I will be seen] in Aeschylus), middle ὁρῶμαι [I see for myself] with aorist εἰδόμην [I saw for myself], whose imperative ἰδοῦ [behold!] has become an interjection ἰδού [behold!], plural ἴδεσθε [behold!], optative ἰδοίμην [may I see for myself] (Doric ἰδοίμαν), infinitive ἰδέσθαι [to see for oneself].
